description: We’re Stellar League, a team brought together by our curiosity about space and our desire to tackle challenges here on Earth. At the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we’ll explore open data, share ideas, and build a prototype together to help understand or solve a real-world problem. Our name is inspired by constellations: it’s the connections between individual stars that bring the bigger picture to life.
summary:
Lunar Odyssey is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12 that trains them to think like a mission commander. Players lead a crew of four across three chapters: build a rocket at a base on the rim of Shackleton crater on the Moon, fly to Mars, and build a new base there that must survive the cold Martian nights.

Every day the crew has fewer batteries than the mission needs, so every choice has a cost: a battery spent on the rocket does not make oxygen or power the radiation shield. Players walk the base, carry batteries to each module and play short hands-on tasks (solar panels, oxygen filters, rover, greenhouse, wiring).

The solar storms are real. The 21 game days replay May 5–25, 2024, the strongest solar storm in two decades, using NASA DONKI events and measured radiation doses from LRO/CRaTER, BioSentinel and Curiosity/MSL-RAD. The ground is real LOLA elevation data, and Mars nights use real Curiosity temperatures.

Kids do not just read about space weather: they make trade-offs under it, and learn that in space no choice is free. Every fact in the game links to its NASA source.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Odyssey is a resource-management adventure game that turns a real space weather event into a mission a 7-year-old can command. The player is the commander of a crew of four astronauts. The goal is to finish three chapters (21 days in total) without letting oxygen or crew health reach zero:

- Chapter 1 – Moon base on the Shackleton crater rim: build the rocket (replays May 5–12, 2024)

- Chapter 2 – Spacecraft: reach Mars (replays May 13–17, 2024)

- Chapter 3 – Mars: build a base from nothing and survive the cold nights (replays May 18–25, 2024)

HOW A DAY WORKS

1. Morning report: mission control tells the player how many batteries they have today and shows a solar storm forecast.

2. Day: the astronaut walks freely around the base, picks up batteries at the Battery Bank and delivers them to modules: Life Support (oxygen), the radiation Shield, the rocket workshop, solar panels, greenhouse and heating. Each module opens a short hands-on task such as cleaning solar panels, swapping a CO2 filter, balancing valves, wiring a circuit or steering the ship. Players can also drive a rover inspired by the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle.

3. Night: the game applies the rules and explains, in short sentences, what went up, what went down and why.

There are always fewer batteries than the mission needs. Shielding for the worst case wastes batteries that could build the rocket; shielding for the best case hurts the crew. During an extreme storm the player has 45 seconds to power the shield. Radiation dose carries from one chapter to the next, so choices on the Moon matter on Mars.

HOW NASA DATA DRIVES THE GAME

- Storms are real. Each day's storm level comes from the measured radiation dose of that exact day, divided by a calm day for the same instrument: LRO/CRaTER in lunar orbit, BioSentinel in deep space and Curiosity MSL-RAD on the surface of Mars (NASA OSDR RadLab).

- Forecasts are uncertain, like real ones. In the morning the player sees only a forecast range built from the DONKI flares, CMEs, particle events and ENLIL runs known on that day. The real level is revealed at night.

- The ground is real. The Moon base sits on LRO LOLA polar elevation data of the Shackleton crater rim. Players can zoom out from the base to the whole Moon (SVS CGI Moon Kit) and to the solar system, with planets in their real positions for each game day (JPL approximate positions) under the real star sky (SVS Deep Star Maps).

- Mars is real. Night heating needs come from Curiosity REMS temperatures.

- Every fact has a source. An in-game "Real NASA data" screen and a wiki link each fact to its NASA page. The game states clearly what is simplified: oxygen, batteries and mission progress are teaching models, not measurements, and the 7-month trip to Mars is shortened to 5 days. Archived data is never shown as live.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Systems thinking for kids: space weather becomes a choice the player must make every day instead of a paragraph to read.

- Real science, honest framing: kids replay a storm that really happened (the May 2024 "Gannon" storm, the strongest in about 20 years) and see the measured numbers behind it.

- Accessible: it runs in any modern browser on desktop, tablet or phone, with no account and no download. It collects no personal data and saves progress locally. Touch controls support tablets. The interface is in English and Portuguese.

- Classroom ready: one game day takes a few minutes, which fits a lesson. Each chapter maps to a topic: life support, radiation, energy, travel and planetary surfaces.

We hope teachers and families use it to start real conversations about how astronauts will live on the Moon and Mars, and that today's kids see themselves as tomorrow's crew.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Game: TypeScript, Phaser 3 and Vite. Static web app with no backend.

- Art: 3D models of the base, rover, spacecraft and astronauts made by the team in Blender and rendered to sprites through Python scripts. Terrain generated from LOLA elevation data.

- Data pipeline: Python scripts download and archive DONKI, RadLab, REMS and LOLA data and convert them into game data files. Every file lists its source links.

- Quality: automated tests (Node test runner) cover the game rules, physics engine, map projection, planet positions and game balance checked against the real May 2024 storm.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- A real, measured solar storm is the game's antagonist, replayed day by day in three places: lunar orbit, deep space and the surface of Mars.

- The gap between the morning forecast and the night reveal turns real space weather prediction into a game mechanic.

- Continuous zoom from an astronaut standing on real lunar terrain out to the whole Moon and then to the solar system.

- No choice is "the safe one": the score rewards balance, not a single optimal path.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Age-appropriate language (short sentences, icons, color-coded bars), scientific honesty (clear notes on what is real and what is simplified), accessibility (runs on low-end devices and phones, no login), privacy (no accounts, no tracking, data saved only in the browser) and openness (public source code and listed data sources).

Github Repo: https://github.com/AdrielCunha/Junior-Astronaut-Mission-Trainer

Team Stellar League.
